title: Issue 57 - How to Tell Your Story
summary:
Your résumé lists what you did. It doesn't explain why it matters or where you're headed. In this issue, you'll build a short story you can say out loud in about 30 seconds that explains who you are, what you offer, and what you're looking to do next.

Have a Better Answer to "Tell Me About Yourself"

"So, tell me about yourself."

It's one of the most common questions you'll face in your career, and one of the hardest to answer well. You hear it in interviews, in promotion conversations, in your first 1:1 with a new manager, and in the hallway at meetups. Most people answer it the same way. They start with their current job and work backward. "Right now I'm at X. Before that, I was at Y..." And the other person's eyes glaze over.

Your résumé lists what you've done, but so does every other candidate's résumé. On paper, you all look equally qualified. Your résumé gets you the interview, but your story explains why your skills matter, how your thinking has evolved to bring you to where you are today, and where you're going next. When you answer with that kind of a story, your listener remembers it long after the conversation ends.

Once you have a story to tell, you can use it everywhere. It works in interviews and networking events, and it also gives you a starting point for your LinkedIn bio, a self-review, or the speaker bio for your next conference talk.

Your story has three parts. Your thread is who you are, your arc is how you've changed over time, and your trajectory is where you're going and why you're ready. Grab a pen or open a notes app, because each part ends with a short writing exercise.

Find your consistent thread

Your thread is the value you bring no matter what job you have. Maybe you're highly organized, or you build strong relationships fast. Maybe you can pick up anything. Your thread is the thing that shows up whether you're writing Go or running a PTA fundraiser.

Your skills are the things you've picked up along the way, and they change all the time. React, Kubernetes, and SQL are skills. Your thread is how you operate, like making messy systems understandable or getting people unstuck, and it'll outlast every framework you ever use. If your thread is "I know React," your story expires the day your team picks a different framework.

"I'm a hard worker" and "I'm passionate about tech" are what everyone says, so they won't help you stand out. A good thread is specific, and it describes something you do. "I turn chaos into processes" tells the listener what to expect when you join their team. So does "I learn the unfamiliar thing fast and teach it to everyone else."

To find your thread, look at what you already do without being asked. Work through these questions to help you find your thread:

  • What do people come to you for, even when it's not your job?
  • What do you do when nobody assigns it?
  • What drains others but energizes you?
  • What compliment do you hear over and over?

If you're not sure, start with the compliment question. If three different managers told you that you ask great questions, you can trust that it's true.

Your thread has to be consistent across your whole life. If you're the one who organizes the team's sprint backlog, you're probably also the one who keeps the family calendar and packs the gear for the camping trip. When you see the same behavior at work and at home, you've found a thread.

So once you have an idea for your thread, test it. Try to point to it in three unrelated places: a job, a different job or school, and something else outside of work. If you can find it in all three, it's your thread. If you can only find it in your current job, you need to keep looking.

Now take two minutes and write one sentence that starts with "I" and a verb. Make sure it holds up in more than one part of your life.

Once you have that, you'll strengthen it by explaining how you got there.

Map your arc

In any good story, the main character changes and grows. That's their arc. Now you have to explain yours.

A list of job titles in order only shows when things happened, like "I was a junior dev, then a mid-level dev, then a senior dev." Compare that to "I used to think my job was to write code. Now I think my job is to solve problems, and code is sometimes the answer." The second example tells you how that person thinks about their work. Your arc should do the same thing.

Characters in stories change because something happens to them that had a profound impact on them, so look for your turning point. It might be a failure or a project that went sideways. A mentor or a manager might have reframed something for you. It might have been a move to a new team or role that gave you a new perspective, or the moment you realized you'd been doing something wrong the whole time. Those are the most believable parts of your story, even if they feel like failures, because they show you can grow from a setback.

Once you've found your turning point, use this template to shape your arc:

I used to [belief or behavior]. Then [turning point]. Now I [new belief or behavior].

You may have more than one of these in your career. Pick the one that best supports where you're going next.

Answer these questions to help you define your arc:

  • What did you believe about your work five years ago that you don't anymore?
  • What can you do now that you couldn't do before?
  • What mistake taught you the most?
  • If you could go back in time, what would you tell yourself on day one of your first job?

Take two minutes and fill in the template. Start with the mistake question if nothing comes to mind. That's a quick way to find a turning point.

Once you've got your arc, you can explain what's next for you and why it's the right move.

Point your story forward

Your thread explains why you're suited to what's next, and your arc explains why you're ready now. Your trajectory names where you're headed. When you tell it well, your next step feels obvious. The listener thinks, "Of course that's next. Look where you've been." Your trajectory gives people a reason to believe in you and what you offer.

That only works if you're specific. "I want to grow as an engineer" and "I want to be a leader someday" don't tell the listener where you're headed. Compare them to this:

I want to own developer experience for an internal platform, because I've spent three years being the person who unblocks everyone else.

Name the problem you want to own or the role you want. Then attach the "because." The "because" is your evidence.

Look for a project where you did the next-level work without the title, or feedback that points toward the new role. Things you built, taught, or led on your own time count too. If you want to be a tech lead, when have you already led? If you want to move into developer education, what have you already taught? If you can't find any evidence, that's useful too. It tells you your next step is to go create some.

These questions will help you find your direction:

  • What problem do you want to own next?
  • What's already pulling you in that direction?
  • What proof do you have today?
  • What's the smallest next step you could take this month?

Take two minutes to name your direction and your evidence. If you only have the direction, write down the evidence you'd need and how you could get it.

Put it together

Now combine your three answers into one short paragraph:

I [thread]. I used to [old], but [turning point], so now I [new]. That's why I'm [next].

Aim for something you can say out loud in about 30 seconds. It'll feel clunky the first time, and that's fine. A draft you can revise beats a blank page.

Here's how it looks for Sam, a hypothetical backend developer:

  • Thread: "I build systems other people can trust."
  • Arc: "I used to measure success by features shipped. Then I was on call for an outage I caused because I wrote code with no tests or alerts. Now I design for failure first."
  • Trajectory: "That's why I'm moving into reliability engineering. I've already led our incident review process and built our alerting playbook."

Sam's thread shows up in the arc, and the trajectory ends with evidence. Anyone who hears this understands why Sam wants a reliability role, and Sam can say it in under a minute. And in an interview, this story can answer some other questions the hiring manager has on their list before they even ask them.

Once you have your story, say it out loud to a friend or a coworker. Then ask them, "What thread did you hear?" If what they heard isn't what you meant, your examples aren't aligned, and you still have work to do.

Keep your story current

You'll tell your story to different people for different reasons, so change what you emphasize based on who's listening. In an interview, emphasize your trajectory so they know why you want this role now. When you're shooting for a promotion, focus on your arc and your evidence. With a new manager, emphasize your thread so they know how to get the best out of you. And at a networking event, keep it short. Share your thread and one line about where you're headed.

Your story will change over time as you grow and face new challenges. Revisit your story every six months or after any big project, especially if you get feedback that changes how you see your work. You should also keep a running list of your wins as they happen. Julia Evans calls this a brag document, and her post includes a template you can start from.

You started with a résumé. Now you have a story. Go tell it to someone.

Things to Explore

  • Video Teleprompter Lite is an iOS app that lets you record videos while displaying the text right on the screen. The front-facing cameras work well on newer phones, so this is a great way to create content on the go while maintaining eye contact with your audience.
  • Paperless-ngx is an open-source document management solution you can use to catalog, search, and manage documents, PDFs, and scans. You can self-host it, and recent versions let you allow LLMs to access your documents. If you want to go paperless but not store your stuff in the cloud, this could be the right solution for you.

Parting Thoughts

Before next month's issue, practice tuning your story for different listeners:

  • Think of two people who'll hear your story in the next few months, like an interviewer and a new manager. Which part of your story should you emphasize for each one? Rewrite your opening sentence for both.
  • Cut your story down to one sentence you could say at a networking event. What did you have to leave out, and does your thread still come through?

As always, thanks for reading.

title: Prompts are not guardrails
summary:
My husband likes to say “prompts aren’t guardrails,” and it’s been ringing in my head for months, so I figured I’d finally write down my take on it.

I regularly see people who are frustrated, or kind of confused, because they told an LLM very emphatically (in ALL CAPS! Repeatedly! Very seriously!) to never do something… and then it did the thing anyway. This shows up in AGENTS.md lines like:

  • ALWAYS FOLLOW THE STYLE GUIDE!
  • Never make an unsigned commit.
  • Do NOT push to main. NEVER PUSH TO MAIN.

I’ve also winced my way through stories of LLMs deleting full production databases or wiping someone’s home directory. The frustration or anger when an LLM does the wrong thing makes sense – we told the computer what not to do, gave it examples of the right thing, and clearly stated how bad it would be if it disobeyed.

But, at the end of the day, the model is a probabilistic token generator with a ton of other stuff in its context window. If something really needs to happen or to not happen, more words and rules aren’t the solution. The rule has to live somewhere that can actually stop the model, which is what “prompts aren’t guardrails” means to me.

Imagining myself doing the LLM’s task

I don’t want to anthropomorphize models, but sometimes imagining myself in a similar situation to the LLM, or trying to do the same task, helps me see a little why something might or might not work. (It’s how I realized that onboarding a human made my AI smarter; if nobody gave me onboarding materials, I wouldn’t understand how to do the job, and I shouldn’t expect differently of an LLM.)

Here’s what I’m imagining in the “prompts aren’t guardrails” scenarios:

Say you asked me to edit a doc, and then handed me a 20-page style guide plus the Chicago Manual of Style and told me to follow all the rules exactly. I can guarantee I would not follow them exactly and would miss a ton of rules. I’d read it and I’d try my best, and I’d still miss things.

If you gave me a list of the most important rules that you cared about, I’d probably get closer to respecting those, but might still drop a few items.

If you instead gave me a tool that tells me every time I’ve violated the style guide, and asked me to get that count to zero, I could do that. The tool does the remembering, and my job becomes fixing whatever it flags.

And if you set things up so that I couldn’t even merge a doc until the style guide violations count was at zero, then it would definitely work out, because the doc has no other way to ship.

The first setup depends on me remembering; the second helps me at least prioritize what to remember; the third tells me when I forgot; and the fourth makes it impossible to ship what I forgot. Only that last one is what I’d call a guardrail, and it’s what’s missing when the model doesn’t obey what you told it to do.

If only words stop it, there isn’t a guardrail

The same thing applies for actions the LLM (or I) should or shouldn’t take. If something should never happen, the system needs to actually prevent it from happening.

Say you don’t want me to SSH into production, but it’s technically possible; I have the keys and nothing is stopping me except the fact that the CTO said everyone needs to seriously stop yeehawing into prod (this may or may not be a real example).

Most days, I’d respect that. However, in the one case where something is broken on prod and SSHing in to fix it would be the fastest path, the rule is something I weigh against the outage and might decide to ignore. The rule and its words, however strongly emphasized, are not the guardrail. If the CTO really wanted me to not do something, the system should have enforced that rather than relying on a memo.

Why was that even allowed?

In blameless postmortem cultures, the goal is to look for the system failure rather than blaming an individual person for their choices. If something broke or something bad happened, why was that thing allowed to happen at all?

If someone on the team ran terraform apply and accidentally took down our whole EC2 cluster (another possibly real life example), the useful question is why anyone was able to do that in the first place, and not why that individual wasn’t more careful with reading the terraform output in this one instance.

This is something that could apply to LLM failures as well. Rather than asking the LLM why it didn’t do something you’d asked it to, it might be better to fix it at the root. This matters even more for a model than for a person. After an incident, a person usually remembers what happened and does better next time, but the model comes in fresh every session. Anything it “learns” from being corrected only sticks if it gets written down somewhere, which puts it right back in words.

If it’s something small that’s more of an annoyance (ex: why didn’t you remind me when the job finished running?), it might be worth rewording your skill or prompt a bit and trying again. But everything you actually care about needs to move out of words and into a deterministic check or a system that doesn’t let it happen at all.

Less convenient, but safer

Guardrails can make things less convenient. Not being able to SSH into prod is annoying, especially when something is broken and you know exactly what to fix. Branch protection means even a one-character typo fix goes through a pull request. Network restrictions mean the model won’t always have everything I might want in its context, but it also isn’t going to send internal data to a random site.

The small annoyances of guardrails add up to a lot fewer incidents. I sometimes hate the extra work I have to do because of them, but ultimately respect and appreciate that we have systems that prevent the “definitely don’t do this” actions. And often the guardrails are built from accidents of the past.

There are ways to make that tradeoff less painful, too. Grant only what the task needs, like a read-only database user for a model that only has to query data, and you keep most of the convenience without the risk of it dropping a table.

Where guardrails can live

If you’re regularly running into issues with a model ignoring what you’re saying, there are lots of places where you could start looking to address root failures outside of the model.

Most of the ones I rely on in my own work are pretty standard CI. Branch and merge protection keep anything from landing on main without a review and passing checks. Vale checks the style guide rules that can be pattern-matched, lychee and mint broken-links catch broken links, and another check looks for anything private that shouldn’t end up public. Here’s where those, and the examples from the top of this post, could live.

If you want…Put the guardrail in…
No pushes to mainBranch protection with required reviews and passing checks, plus a Claude Code permission deny rule or PreToolUse hook that blocks the push before it happens
The style guide followedVale in CI as a required check, plus a Claude Code PostToolUse hook that runs it after every edit so problems show up before CI does
No broken linkslychee or a similar tool in CI as a required check
Nothing private made publicA required CI check that scans for secrets and internal info before merge, plus push protection
Only signed commitsBranch protection that requires signed commits
A task that runs every weekA scheduled job, like a cron job, a GitHub Actions schedule, or a Claude Code routine

For anything running unattended, a sandbox or container bounds what can go wrong to whatever that environment can reach. Network restrictions go a step further by keeping it off networks it has no business touching, like sensitive internal systems or sites you don’t trust.

Side benefit: more room in the context window

Doing some of these can also have the benefit of removing context for the LLM. Instead of spending the context window describing what not to do, just don’t let the bad things happen, and save that space for the things you actually want to tell the LLM.

I used to have our whole style guide in skills and CLAUDE.md, including tons of lines describing deterministic, mechanical rules with examples of right and wrong usage. After adding Vale, I was able to remove all of those. The rules still exist in the Vale config, where they run on every change, and the model only hears about the specific ones it broke. Now the model can focus its attention on the work that takes judgment instead of trying to remember capitalization rules.

Words still matter

None of this means you should stop telling the model what you want. Written instructions are still how it knows what it’s supposed to do, learns your preferences, understands team conventions, etc. But anything you put into words is something the model considers, the same way I’d consider the CTO’s memo about yeehawing into prod when things were on fire. If something truly can’t happen, all the ALL CAPS in the world won’t do what a branch protection rule does.

title: Agent Data Seeking Patterns
summary:
Two conversations this month sent me back into my server logs. The first was the ongoing industry debate about whether llms.txt does anything, which flares up every time a well-known project adds one or removes one. The second was a colleague mentioning that answer engines and crawlers were fetching an llms-info file from their site, which was news to me, because I'd never seen a request for one.

Both are really the same question: what do agents actually reach for when they visit a website? Not what we've told them to reach for, not what the spec du jour says they should reach for, but what shows up in the logs when nobody is watching. I've been running an agent traffic classifier and signal tracker across my sites since April, and it had been a while since I validated the patterns baked into it. So I pulled nine days of logs (September 11 through 19) from twelve sites, re-classified everything, and went looking.

title: What "Just Prompting" Looks Like
summary:
A colleague asked me this week how I've built the things I've built over the past year: the Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec, the afdocs checker, agentsummons and agentminutes, Agent Skill Implementation, the Agent Reading Test. He characterized it as "just prompting," and then asked whether there was something in how I prompt that we could teach non-technical colleagues in his department.

I was skeptical. My private theory was that whatever works for me works because I have enough domain background to notice when the agent is wrong, and that isn't something you can easily hand off. But a private theory is exactly the kind of thing I'd tell an agent to go verify, so I did the same thing to myself. I had Claude Code read every prompt I've given it since December 2025 and tell me what it found.

title: What Technical Writers Actually Do (It’s Not Just Writing)
summary:
Technical writers do more than just type terms. Learn how they bridge information silos and navigate the rise of LLMs.

Most people think the job is just writing technical documentation, but the reality is far more investigative. The role centers on gathering information from fragmented sources like company forums and support tickets to build clear, usable guides. It is a profession that requires connecting the dots between engineering teams and end users who need answers fast.

With over 15 years of experience, I break down how the day-to-day work is shifting. We are moving past traditional methods as LLMs for writers start to reshape how we draft and maintain content. Understanding this evolution is critical for anyone looking to sharpen their content strategy or grow their tech career advice in a modern environment.

title: Writing for an audience of agents — podcast with Ethan Palm from Mintlify
summary: In this podcast, co-host Fabrizio Ferri-Benedetti and I chat with Ethan Palm, a technical writer and knowledge engineer at Mintlify, about what happens when nearly half your documentation traffic comes from AI agents. We discuss Mintlify's platform data on agent versus human traffic, hidden directories for agent-only content, the uncertain future of llms.txt, automated doc maintenance workflows where writing accounts for at most ten percent of the job, and the social atrophy that comes from reaching for a terminal prompt instead of a coworker.
